Your previous sitting's reply:
**Grainstack, Evening** is finished again, now at day 333 on the painting's clock, and my heart is happy with it.

The picture is the same: a big straw stack in violet shadow, with a hot orange rim where the low sun catches its right side. Its long violet shadow falls across gold stubble, and a smaller stack in the distance echoes it. The sky goes from cerulean through rose to lemon, with a pale sun sitting on a hazy line of trees.

**What I changed:** I looked at all of it again, and the only thing that bothered me was the sun disc. In the gallery light its thick paint showed as a crusty disc of horizontal ridges, at the brightest point of the picture.

- **Trials first:** on the scratch canvas I copied the disc and let it dry for 60 days.
  - A painting knife laid over the dry paint failed. It only caught the tops of the ridges and left a raised sliver and a stray line.
  - The same pale paint thinned with oil worked. It filled the furrows and smoothed the surface without changing the colour, and the runnier the mix, the smoother it came out.
- **On the painting:** I laid one coat of the runniest mix over the disc and let it dry for 40 days.
- **Result:** the sun now reads as soft light rather than a crust. A little texture is left, which I'm happy to keep. In normal light its colour is unchanged.

**Weak spots looked at again:**
- **Fine as they are:** the distant stack, last sitting's repair along the main stack's roof edge, the foreground and the hedge line.
- **Accepted as it is:** the broad far end of the cast shadow, because it anchors the lower-left corner.

**Handoff:** everything is dry except the sun's new oily coat, which should be checked before anything goes over it. The journal has the full notes and these lessons:
- **Still holding:**
  - Blend at most one pass.
  - A spirits rag lifts wet paint but leaves a faint streak where each wipe ends.
  - Break up hard-edged masses by painting into them over dry paint.
  - To match a passage, re-mix the recipe from the painting's log.
  - After working near a finished dry outline, wipe inside it while the new paint is wet.
  - To soften an edge, paint thinly over it.
- **New:** a knife can't flatten dry thick paint. An oily coat of the same colour levels it.
- **Hypotheses:** two coats level better than one (from a single trial), and marks spaced evenly along a line tend to read as a fence.

# Paint a picture

Paint one picture of your choosing in oil, at the easel, a simulator of oil
paint on linen. Subject, composition and manner are yours. Your box holds
every tube the studio has, 54 colors: use as many or as few as you like, and
be as bold with color as you want. Work from knowledge and the notes in your
studio; don't use reference images or image models.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint with a rag or a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/every_materials.md (the paints in your box) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.

After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Before adding repeated small details, improve a weakening relationship or deliberately accept it with your reason. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.

Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial, on the scratch canvas beside the painting (`scratch: true`) or on the painting, laid on the intended substrate after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. A held pile shows thick paint on steel; use the laid trial to judge its effect on the picture. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections
  in your journal and finish.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

- day 1, 12:08: Plan: grainstack at sunset, after Monet. Sun low right (~840,372) just above a distant tree line; stack at x 222-546, y 268-636, mostly shadow side toward us (violet), warm rim on the right; long violet cast shadow lower-left. Ground: lead white + ochre + red earth, knifed, warm cream.
  Campaign 1 (day1 09:00-12:08): lay-in of sky (graded piles, broad), trees band, field (graded), stack (body, purple), shadow. Observations: lead-white sky piles came out much paler than wanted - sky washed out, needs a second, more saturated layer. Stack reads as a hut (eave + straight drum walls). Shadow lighter than stack and flat, road-like. Plan: let set ~1.5 days then second campaign over set paint.
- day 21, 08:06: Day 21: Glaze (ultramarine+alizarin+bsienna, medium 0.6) over the dry stack went on in blotchy dark dabs; blending twice made it an even deep purple. Then a hatch of straw_mid/roof_glow 4-wide strokes was too light and hairy; one blend smeared it into flat mauve-brown with a few dark holes. Lesson (hypothesis): the blend hand over two wet layers lifts and averages strongly - one pass is already a lot. Stack now mid-value, no backlit rim, reads hut-like. Next: let dry, then dark transparent glaze on left/centre, hot rim right/top, fix eave notch, rework shadow + foreground stubble, tree band right side muddy.
- day 35, 12:23: Day 32-35: stack repainted wet over dry with 4-pile graded body pass (stack_dk -> stack_plum -> roof_glow -> rim_hot by x across the stack), filbert 6 lay 2.5, coverage 2.5, fill: this worked - reads as straw, warm-to-cool turning form. Eave notch fixed with two small patches + a band of vertical strokes; overhanging straw strokes. Shadow repainted (sh_deep/sh_light) - flat lavender, crisp, path-like. Field: hatch pass of st_lit/st_hot/st_shade scaled with depth (0.6..2.8), coverage 1.1 -> good stubble texture over dry field.
  To do: shadow deeper + modulated, soften its edge with field strokes; tree-line spikes read as crags (reshape); second small distant stack; bright rim on stack's right silhouette; foreground darker/warmer for depth.
- day 52, 14:10: Day 52: shadow glaze gl_sh (ultra+cob violet+alizarin, medium 0.7) over dry lavender shadow -> too saturated, patchy purple, with pale halo where shrink(2) left an untouched rim. Hatch of light stubble piles into it wet -> pale and spotty; one blend -> smooth mauve, too light. Lesson: lighter opaque strokes into a dark wet glaze lighten the whole; for a shadow darker than the lit field, the stubble marks must be darker than the field's darks. Next: once set, darker violet hatch touches in the shadow.
- day 69, 00:51: Day 60-69: distant stack first try blobby - lifted with spirits rag (works on open paint, 3x dipped 0.8, pressure 0.85, removes almost to the dry layer beneath), repainted smaller and rounder. Hedge dashes along horizon too graphic, blended + rag-wiped (ok). Overhang shadow band under eave: eave_sh/stack_dk/eave_warm body strokes then 2 blends -> dark band dissolving downward into straw - reads as overhang. Foreground glaze gl_fg (bsienna+alizarin+cob violet, med 0.75) load ramp 0.25..0.7 with y, blended once: warm orange-red depth, good.
  Remaining: cast shadow is a flat straight-edged band (path-like) -> give it a darker core near the stack, fading/broken far end; backlit rim along stack's right/top silhouette; sun glow more luminous.
- day 175, 08:29: Day 145-175, finishing. A contact shadow ribbon under the drum came out as a hard purple ring; blending smeared it into a slab, and the spirits rag left two lines. I repainted it as lit stubble on the right and shadow running up to the base on the left, plus one thin dark gesture under the lit right side. That fixed it. Signed "CA" lower right in eave_warm. Waited 30 days.
  Reflection: the picture works as one evening chord: violet stack and shadow against gold stubble and a lemon-to-rose-to-cerulean sky, with the sun low on the right picked out in the straw along the stack's edge. The best passage is the stack, painted with graded multi-pile body strokes over dry paint. What it taught me: the blend hand is strong (one pass is plenty), and lifting with a spirits rag before the paint sets is the real undo. Weak spots I'm accepting: the cast shadow is still a bit band-like and even in width, the foreground glaze is blotchy, and the far field edge is a pale line.
- day 175, 08:53: Sitting 2 (day 175). Fresh look: the picture holds. Weak spots carried over: (1) the cast shadow is an even-width band with smooth edges, (2) the foreground glaze is patchy, (3) there's a pale line at the far field edge.
  (1) Fixed today, over dry paint: noise-thresholded "bays" of lit stubble hatched into the shadow's edges (st_hot/f_deep/st_lit/f_gold, cov 1.6) and "tongues" of shadow hatch pushed out into the field (sh_dk2/sh_mid2/sh_plum). Width now varies and the edges are ragged like stubble. Then a sparse hatch of sh_plum (cobalt violet 1, alizarin .3, bsienna .3, ultra .15, white .35) at cov 0.4 over the shadow's interior gives warm plum marks over the blue-violet. I tried it on scratch first, over a dried sh_core/sh_mid2 hatch: sh_plum reads as a darker warm accent. sh_rose (with vermilion) was too pink and light, and Mars orange/violet came out a chalky salmon.
- day 215, 10:49: Day 175-215, sitting 2 continued. Here is my verdict on each weakness I'd flagged:
  (1) Band-like cast shadow: IMPROVED. On dry paint I hatched lit-stubble bays into the shadow and pushed shadow tongues out into the field, both shaped by noise thresholds on a blurred shadow mask (blur 36, threshold amplitude 0.42, period 90). The first try (blur 22, amplitude 0.32) changed too little to see. Then a sparse sh_plum hatch went over the interior. The shadow now narrows and widens, and its edges are ragged like stubble. Its far end at the lower left is still broad, and I'm accepting that because it anchors the corner.
  (2) Patchy foreground glaze: IMPROVED. I left the glaze alone and hatched sparse body strokes over the dry foreground: st_hot/f_deep/eave_warm/st_lit/sh_plum at cov 0.55 from y 630, then f_deep/eave_warm/sh_plum at cov 0.4 from y 690. That turns the blotches into deliberate red-orange stubble that deepens toward the bottom edge.
  (3) Pale line at the far field edge: IMPROVED. A fine vertical-dash hatch (round 2) went along the foot of the trees, with a field strip under it, then one horizontal blend. That gives a soft hazy edge on the right. On the left, tr_dark/sh_mid2 dashes and a blend made a darker violet hedge line, which sits better behind the stack and makes the field edge read.
  Lesson (hypothesis, but it held twice): to break a hard-edged mass, carve it with the opposite paint over the DRY layer using noise-thresholded masks, rather than blending wet. The blend averages, while hatching over dry paint keeps the marks.
  Note on looking: in gallery light the sun disc shows its impasto ridges. I'm leaving that as it is.
  Reflection: my heart is happy with this. Tying the shadow into the stubble has made the whole lower half feel like one field. The stack still carries the picture. Signed and finished.
  HANDOFF (if ever reopened): globals still alive: shadow4_m, stack2_m, field_m, sky_m, treeband_m, pops_m, ds_m, sun_x/sun_y. Everything is dry by day 215. The blend hand is strong (one pass is plenty). Lifting with a spirits rag (dip 0.8, pressure 0.8, 2-3 rounds) only works on open paint. Before a new mix goes on, try it on scratch over a dried underlayer of the same paint.
- day 247, 12:04: Sitting 3 (day 215-247). On a fresh look, the distant stack read as a blob (rounded dome on a narrow foot) and the lit field right of centre was all gold, with no shadow colour tying it to the stack and the cast shadow.
    (a) Distant stack: IMPROVED. Over dry paint I painted out the old dome flanks below y 470 with field piles (detail, filbert 2.5), then repainted the stack as two drawn shapes. dcap_m is a wider, flatter cone with eaves at about 700-766. ddrum_m is a drum inset from it (705-759, y 468-494). I used the same graded piles as the big stack (d_dk/d_plum/d_glow/d_rim, all copies of ds_dk/stack_plum/roof_glow/rim_hot). After 12 days dry I added a thin eave line (d_eave fading to eave_warm), darkened the top of the drum with d_drum (mixed from d_dk .6, d_eave .25, d_plum .15), and put a rim-light gesture on its right edge and a short shadow to the left. It now echoes the main stack and reads as a grainstack at distance. One thing doesn't fit: the overhang band blended pale for a moment. One blend pass over 4-day-open paint lifted it, which confirms again that blending is strong.
    (b) Violet flecks in the right field: NEW, kept. I tried three piles on scratch (dry gold hatch, sparse hatch cov 0.15, load 0.5): sh_mid2 came out blue-violet, st_shade plum, and f_lav pale lilac. All were too crisp and spotty laid as they were. Wiping the wet flecks once with a rag (dip 0.4, pressure 0.45, one pass) broke them into half-lifted plum flecks. A blend smeared them into lilac clouds, which I rejected. On the painting I used st_shade 1 + sh_mid2 0.4, cov 0.12, load lighter in the sun lane, y 500-720, then the same rag wipe. The flecks carry the shadow colour across the lit field without breaking it up.
    Re-judged the old items: the far broad end of the cast shadow is still ACCEPTED (it anchors the corner). The foreground stubble and the hedge line are fine as they are.
    Lesson (hypothesis, one trial plus one use): sparse dark flecks over a dry light field look stamped on. A light spirits-rag wipe while they're wet breaks them into the texture, and is better than blending.
    Reflection: I'm happy with it. The second stack now rhymes with the first, and the field has a little of the evening's violet in it. Finished at day 247.
    HANDOFF: everything is dry by day 247. New globals: dcap_m, ddrum_m, dnew_m (the distant stack), plus the d_* piles. The older globals are as listed before. Practical lessons: blend at most one pass; lift wet paint with a spirits rag; carve hard masses over DRY paint with the opposite colour; try new mixes on scratch over a dried underlayer first.
- day 247, 12:49: Sitting 4 (day 247). Fresh look: the main stack's eave was a ruled straight dark band with a regular row of short dark vertical ticks above it (the "overhanging straw" strokes from chunk 46). Up close it read as a picket fence, and the straight line flattened the drum.
    Trials on scratch over a dried roof/band/ticks underlayer: (1) pointed round-3 strands hanging over the band looked like fangs, a worse fence. (2) Blunt filbert-5 strands at 4-8 spacing were still a fence: evenly spaced parallel marks along a line always read as pickets. (3) WORKED: a skirt of short filbert strokes laid along the roof's fall direction in a band 16-27 units deep above a new eave line that sags 6 units at the centre (yEave(x) = 500 + 6(1-u^2), u = (x-373)/140), then a dark band 7→4 thick along the arc.
    On the painting the first skirt went on in d_dk/d_plum/d_glow. Those are the distant stack's aerial piles, heavy in white, so they dried to a pale pink stripe over the darker roof. I lifted it while open with a spirits rag (dip 0.8-1.0, pressure 0.9, 3+2 passes, width 14): almost clean, with a faint haze and a streak line at the top of the wipe. A second trial in sk_blue (d_dk + d_eave + sh_mid2) came out pale lilac and was lifted too. Third trial, re-knifed from the original recipes in the log: stack_dk (ultra 1, aliz .5, cob violet 1, bsienna .5, white .5) plus eave_sh toward the band. That matched the value. Full skirt: filbert 3, length 8-18, coverage 1.5, angle along the fall, mask from a-27 to a, roughened, piles graded by x: stack_dk → stack_plum → d_glow (= roof_glow) → d_rim (= rim_hot), with eave_sh rising toward the band. RESULT: the eave reads as thatch turning under, with a curved shadow line and a ragged straw edge. The ticks are gone.
    Lessons: (a) to match an existing passage, re-knife the recipe it was actually painted with (it's in the log), not a lookalike pile; whiter piles over a glazed dark passage read much lighter. (b) Hypothesis: evenly spaced parallel marks along a line make a fence. Strokes that follow the form's own direction and overlap the line do better.
- day 263, 12:54: Day 263, end of sitting 4. After 16 days the skirt was dry. A faint pale streak was left where the rag wipe had stopped (y ≈ a-30, x 280-330). I covered it over the dry paint with a sparse band of fall-direction strokes in stack_dk/stack_plum (filbert 3, coverage 0.9, mask a-34..a-20, x 236-440). Now it's invisible.

    - Main stack eave: IMPROVED (see above). It now reads as thatch turning under.
    - Distant stack: ACCEPTED. Its eave is a flat line with small ticks, but at that size it reads correctly as a distant stack.
    - Broad far end of the cast shadow: still ACCEPTED, because it anchors the lower-left corner.
    - Foreground stubble, hedge line, violet flecks in the lit field: fine as they are.
    - The sun disc's impasto in gallery light: ACCEPTED.
    Reflection: my heart is happy. The eave fix was small but it was the last mechanical-looking passage on the main stack, and it now has the same handling as the rest of the roof. Finished at day 263.

Piles re-knifed this sitting: stack_dk, stack_plum, eave_sh, sk_dk, sk_mid, sk_blue (the last three are unused and lighter than they look). Practical lessons (still holding): blend at most one pass. A spirits rag (dip 0.8-1.0, pressure 0.8-0.9, several passes) is the undo for open paint, but it leaves a faint streak where each wipe ends. Carve hard masses over dry paint with the opposite colour. Try new mixes on scratch over a dried underlayer. NEW: to match a passage, re-knife the recipe from the log. Hypothesis: evenly spaced parallel marks along a line read as a fence.
- day 293, 13:31: Sitting 5 (day 263-293). Fresh look: the whole picture holds. Two weak spots around the DISTANT stack that I hadn't seen before: (1) a faint rectangle of finer, smoother field marks round it, left over from the day-247 repaint (rect(694,466,78,30) + rect(696,429,74,10)), with a straight vertical seam at x≈695; (2) a "cupcake" drum: rounded-in bottom corners and a scalloped dark foot over pale field.

FAILED: it made a stepped notch, and the pale stubble block cut up into the drum. I lifted it while wet with a rag (width 10, dip 0.9, pressure 0.85, 2x2 passes). That left only a faint haze.

RESULT: the rectangle seam is gone and the base sits in stubble. BUT the hatch strokes overshoot their mask and nibbled the cap silhouette and the orange eave rim. While they were wet, a rag wiped inside dnew_m only (width 8, dip 0.9, pressure 0.85, 3x2 passes, angle vertical). That restored the silhouette, because the dry stack underneath stays put. After 8 days dry I put the rim back with round-2 d_rim/d_glow gestures down the right slope, at the eave tip and on the drum edge.

    Lessons: (a) hatch strokes overshoot their mask by about half a stroke length. Near a finished dry silhouette, plan a rag wipe inside the silhouette mask straight afterwards; it lifts only the new wet paint. (b) Extending a form's corner plus a pale strip under it reads as a notch. Breaking an edge works better by overlapping it thinly than by re-drawing it. (c) Confirmed again: re-knifing the log recipe matches the surrounding passage.
    Reflection: my heart is happy. These were small repairs, but the distant stack was the last place where a repaint still showed its own outline. Finished at day 293.

Practical lessons that still hold: blend at most one pass; a spirits rag is the undo for open paint and leaves a faint streak where a wipe ends; carve hard masses over dry paint with the opposite colour; re-knife from the log to match; try new marks small first and lift them if they fail; wipe inside a dry silhouette after hatching near it. Hypothesis: evenly spaced marks along a line read as a fence.

**Grainstack, Evening** is finished again, now at day 395 on the painting's clock, and my heart is happy with it.

The picture is unchanged in its essentials: a big straw stack in violet shadow, with a hot orange rim where the low sun catches its right side. Its long violet shadow falls across gold stubble, and a smaller stack echoes it in the distance. The sky runs from cerulean through rose to lemon, with a pale sun sitting on a hazy line of poplars.

**What I changed:** looking closely, I found the poplars striped with a pale gold crackle. An old sky glaze had collected in the grooves of their dry paint, and it made them look moth-eaten.
- **Trials first:** on the scratch canvas I recreated the problem, then tried three ways to cover it.
  - Fluid, oily paint came out flat and airbrushed.
  - A violet glaze pooled into purple veins.
  - Re-mixing the poplars' original paint from the painting's log and laying it on lightly in strokes worked.
- **On the painting:** I used that third method on the poplars and the haze band.
- **Result:** the poplars now read as solid, soft violet shapes.

**Two failed attempts:** I tried twice to warm the cooler haze to the right of the sun.
- A blended hatch flattened into a buff slab with a hard top edge.
- A glaze pooled into an ochre blot.

I wiped both off with a spirits rag while they were wet, and they came off cleanly. I'm accepting that cooler haze as it is, because at full size it reads as distance falling out of the sun's glare.

**Weak spots looked at again:**
- **Fine as they are:** the distant stack, the main stack's roof edge, the foreground, the hedge line, and the sun's surface, which is now dry and smooth.
- **Accepted as it is:** the broad far end of the cast shadow, because it anchors the lower-left corner.

**Handoff:** everything is dry at day 395, and the journal has the full notes. These are the lessons to carry forward:
- **Still holding:**
  - Blend at most one pass, and never over a fresh, sparse hatch.
  - A spirits rag lifts wet paint cleanly back to the dry layer underneath, but leaves a faint streak where each wipe ends.
  - Break up hard-edged masses by painting into them over dry paint.
  - To match or cover a passage, re-mix its recipe from the log.
  - Try new marks on scratch first, over a dried underlayer.
  - After working near a finished dry outline, wipe inside it while the new paint is wet.
  - To flatten dry thick paint, use a runny coat of the same colour, not a knife.
- **New:** a glaze blended over dry, textured paint gets caught in the grooves as crackle. Lightly re-laying the original paint covers it.
- **Hypotheses:**
  - Glazes in narrow bands pool.
  - Two runny coats level better than one.
  - Marks spaced evenly along a line tend to read as a fence.
